computed: peak = base peak + sensitivity × degrees below

OPS:0.title: What a frequency trend is evidence of
OPS:0.takeaway: Frequency is a system-wide balance signal; its rate of change depends on both the power mismatch and stored kinetic energy.
assumes: an alternating supply has a frequency measured in cycles per second

GEN:0.title: How much power actually left the system
GEN:0.takeaway: The initial rate of frequency change measures the size of the imbalance, given the inertia.
assumes: a rate of change can be read off the steep part of a trend

METER:0.title: The order the records claim things happened in
METER:0.takeaway: Agreement is independent evidence only when the channels do not share the same dependency.
assumes: a timestamp combines a measured event with a clock reference
two channels can agree because they share the same source

TRANS:0.title: What you do before a relay does it for you
TRANS:0.takeaway: A protection plan must be written before the number moves, with earlier thresholds for actions that take longer to arrive.
assumes: continuous and emergency ratings are different limits
redispatch is slower than automatic or operator load shedding

LOAD:0.title: The power that never arrives
LOAD:0.takeaway: Loss rises with the square of current, which is why a small overload costs more than it looks.
assumes: current through a resistance dissipates power as heat

OPS:1.title: The contingency you are actually protecting against
OPS:1.takeaway: A rating is only interesting alongside what the flow does when that element is gone.
assumes: a network is required to survive the loss of any single element

DIST:0.title: Why the far end sits low
DIST:0.takeaway: Volt drop is set by the current and by both parts of the line's impedance.
assumes: current flowing through a resistance produces a drop in voltage

TRANS:1.title: What actually limits a conductor
TRANS:1.takeaway: Current sets the heat, voltage sets the insulation, and the two limits are separate.
assumes: a conductor warms up as current passes through it

OPS:2.title: The order somebody will read back to you
OPS:2.takeaway: The first crew goes where the consequence of waiting is worst, not where the count is biggest.
assumes: a crew can only work one fault at a time

METER:1.title: What three phases actually add up to
METER:1.takeaway: Three-phase power from line quantities carries a factor of root three, and it is not three.
assumes: a three-phase supply carries power on three conductors at once

GEN:1.title: Four things that have to agree before the breaker closes
GEN:1.takeaway: Speed, then voltage, then phase angle, and only then the breaker.
assumes: a generator joined to a live system is forced to turn at the system's speed

TRANS:2.title: Two instruments, two quantities
TRANS:2.takeaway: Peak and RMS are different quantities, and one is the other divided by root two.
assumes: an alternating voltage changes continuously through each cycle

LOAD:1.title: What comes out against what went in
LOAD:1.takeaway: Round-trip efficiency is measured on the energy, not on the power rating.
assumes: storing energy and recovering it both lose some of it

GEN:2.title: The reason the wires are not at wall voltage
GEN:2.takeaway: The same power can be delivered in more than one way, and the ways are not equally wasteful.
assumes: a transformer changes voltage in proportion to its turns

OPS:3.title: What is worth knowing before the peak
OPS:3.takeaway: The value of a measurement is the decision it can change, not how precise or interesting it sounds.
assumes: reserve is held against uncertainty rather than only the forecast centre
storage power and storage deliverability are separate claims

TRANS:3.title: How the flow splits between two paths
TRANS:3.takeaway: The lower-impedance path takes the larger share, in inverse proportion.
assumes: two paths between the same two points carry the same voltage across them

OPS:4.title: What a node has to add up to
OPS:4.takeaway: A conservation law bounds the parts of a system without identifying any of them.
assumes: charge does not accumulate at a junction

DIST:1.title: What is common and what divides
DIST:1.takeaway: Series shares the current and divides the voltage; parallel shares the voltage and divides the current.
assumes: a circuit can be connected end to end or side by side

TRANS:4.title: What a short circuit is limited by
TRANS:4.takeaway: Fault current is the driving voltage over the impedance of the path, and nothing else limits it.
assumes: a short circuit leaves almost no impedance in the path

METER:2.title: A reading taken without a connection
METER:2.takeaway: A current transformer responds to changing magnetic flux; a steady primary current produces no sustained secondary signal.
assumes: a changing magnetic field can induce voltage in a nearby coil
the bench current transformer has 1 primary turn and 20 secondary turns

DIST:2.title: The ground is not at one voltage
DIST:2.takeaway: Isolation is not proof of safety, and earthing is what makes it provable.
assumes: a conductor can be re-energised from more than one direction

LOAD:2.title: The peak, and how far the cold moves it
LOAD:2.takeaway: A forecast is a base shape plus a sensitivity, and the sensitivity is measured rather than assumed.
assumes: demand rises as the temperature falls, roughly in step
computes: peak = base peak + sensitivity × degrees below

OPS:5.title: Cheapest first, and the exceptions that are not exceptions
OPS:5.takeaway: Merit order is cost order, corrected for what the system also needs from a machine.
assumes: generation is scheduled in order of what it costs to run

GEN:3.title: When the cheapest power cannot get out
GEN:3.takeaway: Curtailment is what a network limit looks like from the generator's end.
assumes: power has to have a path to where it is used

OPS:6.title: Why the island's frequency is falling slowly
OPS:6.takeaway: A frequency slope constrains the ratio of power imbalance to stored kinetic energy; it does not determine either one by itself.
assumes: the island is near 50 Hz
the initial frequency slope follows df/dt = f₀ΔP/(2E_k)

METER:3.title: What is stored, and for how long
METER:3.takeaway: Every store has a timescale, and matching the store to the timescale is the whole trick.
assumes: energy can be stored in a spinning mass, in a magnetic field or in a chemical cell

DIST:3.title: Keeping it, or collapsing it on purpose
DIST:3.takeaway: Shedding some load to keep an island alive is usually cheaper than restoring it from nothing.
assumes: restoring a collapsed island takes longer than holding a live one

GEN:4.title: What the dark hours actually cost
GEN:4.takeaway: Power is a rate and energy is the amount, and the settlement is always in energy.
assumes: power sustained over a period of time delivers energy

OPS:7.title: The order physics allows
OPS:7.takeaway: A black start is a dependency chain: the largest generator is useless until a smaller source can energise its auxiliaries through a complete path.
assumes: the large station needs electrical auxiliaries before it can start
the hydro unit can start without an outside electrical supply

DIST:4.title: Why it cannot go faster
DIST:4.takeaway: Every restoration step is limited by something different, and hurrying the wrong one collapses it again.
assumes: a small live system is disturbed more by a given block of load than a large one

METER:4.title: The sensor that was confident and wrong
METER:4.takeaway: Precision is repeatability; accuracy is being right. A drifted sensor has the first and not the second.
assumes: an instrument can be precise and still be offset from the truth

TRANS:5.title: What a rating is a statement about
TRANS:5.takeaway: A rating is a temperature expressed as a current, so a wrong temperature makes the current limit meaningless.
assumes: a conductor's rating is a limit on temperature rather than on current
resistive heating rises faster than the current that causes it

OPS:8.title: What survives a bad number
OPS:8.takeaway: A bad input invalidates what rested on it and leaves the rest standing, and telling them apart is the work.
assumes: a conclusion can depend on one input or on several

OPS:9.title: The failure that has not happened
OPS:9.takeaway: An N-1 check is a statement about single failures, and it says nothing about 2.
assumes: a system is required to survive any one credible failure

LOAD:3.title: The trend with nothing wrong with it
LOAD:3.takeaway: One good night is not evidence about the method, because the width was never a claim about tonight.
assumes: a forecast can be right by luck as easily as by skill on any one day

GEN:5.title: Which of these is a measurement
GEN:5.takeaway: An old assumption deserves priority when it is load-bearing, likely to have changed, and cheap enough to check.
assumes: stored kinetic energy affects the initial rate of frequency change
inverter-connected generation may add power without adding synchronous inertia

OPS:10.title: Which of the three cannot wait
OPS:10.takeaway: Urgency comes from how fast a condition is worsening, how reversible it is, and whether somebody else can own the next move.
assumes: a stable problem can be severe without becoming more urgent each minute
reserve actions need lead time before the peak

TRANS:6.title: Loss when the load turns up anyway
TRANS:6.takeaway: When a quantity enters squared, a small change in it is a large change in the result.
assumes: loss in a conductor rises with the square of the current

LOAD:4.title: An order that survives being carried out
LOAD:4.takeaway: Do the moves that improve your information first and the moves you cannot undo last.
assumes: some actions change the value of the actions that follow them

METER:5.title: Hours over limit, added up
METER:5.takeaway: Thermal damage integrates over time, so 90 scattered hours count as 90 hours.
assumes: time spent above a thermal limit accumulates rather than resetting

TRANS:7.title: What the window is worth
TRANS:7.takeaway: When one path closes today, its value includes everything the eighteen-month delay would cost.
assumes: an option with an expiry date is worth more than the same option without one

OPS:11.title: The 18 months you just bought
OPS:11.takeaway: Committing to a fix commits you to running the system without it until it arrives, and that has to be planned too.
assumes: a decision to build something is also a decision about the years before it exists

METER:6.title: Measured, inferred, assumed
METER:6.takeaway: A signed claim is still only as strong as the evidence behind it; verification should go first to critical claims that remain unbacked.
assumes: a report claim can be measured, inferred or still assumed
verification time is limited before the report closes

LOAD:5.title: The number that has to be a range
LOAD:5.takeaway: A prediction is only usable by a planner if it says how wrong it might be.
assumes: a forecast is a distribution rather than a single value

OPS:12.title: What outlives the emergency
OPS:12.takeaway: Keep the practices that would have caught the fault early, and drop the ones that only paid off because the fortnight was abnormal.
assumes: a practice adopted under pressure has a cost that only shows up later
